item.title: Self-hosting got dramatically easier this year, and coding agents are the reason
item.itunes:title: Self-hosting got dramatically easier this year, and coding agents are the reason
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Self-hosting sounds fun on paper, but if the app you want to self-host doesn't have an easy Docker setup, the whole process can leave you scratching your head, especially if you're not comfortable with databases and code. I once tried to set up live TV channels in Jellyfin using ErsatzTV, and getting it running on my Mac turned into a much bigger project than I expected. I ended up configuring everything manually, including an Elasticsearch search index. I remember how intense that night got and how much verbal abuse my MacBook had to endure.

Since then, I've learned a lot about self-hosting and can usually work my way around complicated setups. What has helped even more is using coding agents to do much of the work for me. I use both Claude Code and Codex, and I can ask either tool to handle setup or troubleshoot problems. For example, I recently added a bunch of features I'd always wanted in Karakeep. The developers hadn't shipped them, so I asked Codex to fork the open-source project and implement those features in my own version. The point is, in 2026, decent hardware and a capable coding agent remove most technical barriers to self-hosting, even if you don't know how to code.

You can just ask your coding agent to self-host something for you

And it will do that well

I pay $20 a month for ChatGPT Plus, which gives me access to Codex and features like Computer Use. Once you enable this feature and grant it the necessary permissions, Codex can interact with apps on your device, click buttons, navigate menus, and do things the same way you would. You no longer have to take a screenshot, send it to Codex, and ask it to walk you through the process. It's also no longer limited to writing YAML files and scripts for you. It can handle the entire process from start to finish.

Let's take a simple example of installing Jellyfin on this MacBook. Say you're someone who's just starting out with self-hosting media servers and you already have a collection of movies and TV shows on your laptop. You can simply ask Codex or Claude Code to set up a media server using those files. The agent can organize your media into a folder structure that Jellyfin recognizes, install and configure the server on your Mac, set up the web interface, and create a user account. Once everything is ready, it can give you a local URL and credentials to log in. You don't even have to understand how the whole installation process works. You just open the URL in your browser, log in, and start watching. If you don't like how things look, you can ask Codex to install compatible plugins and customize the interface.

This's a rather simple example. I've had success with much more complicated setups, including connecting Home Assistant with Node-RED. I wanted to use Node-RED to build more complex automations that were difficult to create and manage through Home Assistant's default automation editor. So I asked Codex to install Node-RED on my device, connect it to my existing Home Assistant setup, and build the automations I wanted.

Codex went ahead and set up Node-RED, connected it to Home Assistant, and explored my entire smart home configuration to understand the available devices, entities, and integrations. Once it had a clear picture of how everything was connected, I described the automation I wanted in natural language, and it built the entire flow for me in Node-RED. I didn't have to manually connect nodes, figure out the right entities, or write any code myself.

6 lessons I learned after ditching Plex for Jellyfin on my NAS

A self-hosted setup that finally feels mine

By  Karandeep Singh

Coding agents have revolutionized troubleshooting for me

They can fix things in minutes

A few years ago, back in 2023, whenever I tried self-hosting something, I could usually get the installation right. What deterred me from using these setups seriously was maintenance and troubleshooting. Initially, a self-hosted app would work fine for a few days, but sooner or later, something would break. That's usually when I'd abandon the setup because I had no idea how to fix it.

If you're not particularly tech-savvy, troubleshooting errors involving databases, containers, and other components of a self-hosted setup can be difficult. Back then, documentation for specific configurations was often limited, so you had to rely on community forums for help. If nobody had encountered the same problem or bothered to respond to your question, you were stuck trying to figure it out yourself.

Coding agents have changed that forever. They can diagnose and fix errors in minutes. When a container crashes or a port is blocked, you no longer have to spend hours searching through forums. You can simply give the agent access to your setup, and it can inspect the error logs, identify the problem, and fix it.

For example, let's say your Jellyfin Docker container suddenly refuses to start because another application is already using port 8096. You could spend an hour figuring out why Jellyfin isn't accessible, looking through Docker logs, and searching for similar issues online. With Codex, you can simply ask it to investigate why Jellyfin isn't working. It can inspect the container logs, check which application is occupying the port, update the port mapping in your Docker Compose configuration, and restart the container. It can even verify that Jellyfin is accessible again before telling you the problem has been resolved.

And this extends to more complicated issues involving broken dependencies, database connections, and configuration errors. You don't have to understand every component of your self-hosted setup to keep it running anymore.

Your agent can manage an entire server remotely

SSH makes remote management much easier

One of the best things about coding agents is that they don't even need to run on the same machine as your self-hosted applications. If you have a NAS, a mini PC, or an old laptop running a bunch of services, you can simply give Codex or Claude Code SSH access to that machine and have it manage everything remotely. I've already used Codex over SSH to inspect my NAS, and it's surprising how much work you can get done without manually touching the server.

Let's say you have a NAS running Jellyfin and want to add another self-hosted application. You can ask the agent to connect to the NAS, inspect the existing Docker containers, check the available resources, and figure out how to install the new application without disrupting anything already running. It can create the necessary Docker Compose files, configure persistent storage, install dependencies, and bring the service online. If you want to access that application securely over the internet, it can also help configure a reverse proxy, set up your domain, and provision an SSL certificate through Let's Encrypt.

You can even have the agent manage multiple machines. For example, if you're running Jellyfin on your NAS and Home Assistant on a mini PC, the agent can connect to both machines over SSH and handle tasks across them. You don't have to keep switching between terminal sessions or remember where every configuration file is stored.

Self-hosting is now for everyone

A few years ago, setting up and maintaining all of this required a fair amount of Linux knowledge, patience, and time spent reading documentation. Now, you can describe what you want in plain English and let the agent handle the technical work. And that's precisely what makes self-hosting so much more accessible in 2026.

I built a self‑hosted Netflix with Jellyfin, Emby, and Plex, and only one was the clear winner

It's worth trying all self-hosted media platforms, but there is a best fit.

item.title: I found an off-grid open source VPN, and it's amazing
item.itunes:title: I found an off-grid open source VPN, and it's amazing
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Our increasingly connected world runs on several layers of networking stacks that help route, find, and receive data from external sources. But that's not the only way to communicate digitally, even if the IP-based networking stack that runs the internet is the generally accepted method. There are many compromises in its design, tracing back to the origin of the Internet Protocol, and there are other ways to do things.

Decentralized mesh networks are one, and if you've used any of the next-gen VPN solutions like Tailscale or ZeroTier, you have some idea of what I'm talking about. These solutions still layer new protocols over the accepted IP-based network stack, but other ways exist to achieve the same goal.

One is called Reticulum, an open-source, cryptography-based network stack. It's the protocol and transport layers for making secure, decentralized, and resilient local or wide-area networks, designed to be medium-agnostic, in that it works on almost any transmission medium that could reliably pass a few bytes at a time. It's pretty neat, but tricky to use on its own, but that's what the VPN built on top of the Reticulum stack handles for you.

What is Reticulum anyway?

And why do we need another networking stack?

Reticulum uses existing hardware, like LoRa radios, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, serial lines or anything else that can pass data and turns it into a mesh-based network stack. But it can also be used over external programs, or piped over existing IP networks, so it's completely medium agnostic. While traditional networking uses IP allocations for addressing individual devices, Reticulum uses a concept of destinations, which are defined using cryptographic keys.

It doesn't require centralized infrastructure, can be designed as open or needs authentication to join the mesh, and uses full end-to-end encryption for data in transit. It needs no drivers, no kernel modules, and runs on anything Python 3 can run, making it a fully software-defined networking solution.

Differences from the traditional network stack:

Feature

Traditional TCP/IP Network

Reticulum Network

Addressing

IP addresses, central allocation

Cryptographic keys / destinations

Topology

Usually hierarchical or client-server

True mesh, flat, peer-to-peer

Encryption

Optional, app-dependent

Always-on, enforced at protocol level

Sender privacy

Weak, source address visible

Strong, sender can be anonymous

Routing

Static, centrally coordinated

Self-discovering, multi-hop, dynamic

Medium

IP only (Ethernet/Wi-Fi)

Any channel: LoRa, serial, radio, etc.

Control/Censorship Resistance

Vulnerable to central shutoff

Highly resilient, no global “off switch”

Setup/Admin

Requires admin, often complex

Userland, minimal, DIY-friendly

It's also low-bandwidth, designed to work on anything with a half-duplex channel with 5 bits per second and MTU of 500 bytes as a minimum. That adds radios and a whole scope of low-power IoT devices into the mix for the mesh, making it great for off-grid messaging, remote sensors, disaster response, or anyone who could benefit from a decentralized, encrypted network.

It's built to be secure with initiator anonymity

Because cryptographic keys identify nodes on the network, nothing else about the device being used, the user using it, or anything else that might identify it is passed on across the network. All communications are secured by ECDH X25519 key exchange, with AES-128/256 encryption. The network doesn't reveal anything about the identity of the sender of a message by default and design, making this secure by design and without the overhead and cruft of IP networking.

Reticulum is pretty neat on its own

Reticulum doesn't need much to get going, with a simple pip package manager command to install:

pip install rns

or pipx as it was on my Ubuntu install.

That's all it takes to get Reticulum running on your device, but then what programs can you use with it? Well, there's Nomad Network which is a spy thriller-esque encrypted communications suite that has synchronous, asynchronous, and file-sharing capabilities. Or the GUI-based Reticulum MeshChat app that works on macOS and Windows.

That's only the surface of what you can do, and remember, these apps don't need any connections to the public internet to work. They don't even need Ethernet, or IP networks, or any existing network functionality at all.

Reticulum
See at Github See at Official Site

But there's more utility to be found

Reticulum with a P2P VPN over the top makes it work with existing software

Credit: Source: Wikimedia Commons

Now that we've got a completely new software-defined networking stack, we can do all kinds of things with it. The rns-vpn project builds a P2P VPN over the Reticulum mesh network, which had me scratching my head for a minute because it adds encryption again on top of an already encrypted network, until I realized why.

The extra encryption is to preserve the privacy-by-design of Reticulum while adding a static IP address to each node in the mesh. This keeps you private, but lets the users use existing IP-based tools to communicate, as you can reach each peer with its assigned IP address.

The configuration file for this basically has a list of the cryptographic LXMF address that Reticulum uses and an assigned IP address for the VPN to use:

vpn_ip = "10.0.0.1/24"

[peers]
"10.0.0.2" = "xxx"

An LXMF address looks like 4faf1b2e0a077e6a9d92fa051f256038, and would go where the xxx is in the config file. The neat thing is that because it's a hash, you can have multiple devices on the network with the same app or device name, because the destination hash will still be unique.

This is similar to ZeroTier in many ways

Using a VPN over Reticulum is similar to how ZeroTier works over an IP-based internet stack, in that you can transparently route traffic over the mesh to individual clients, without needing to add your own networking code to your applications. It's a little different in that the VPN over Reticulum lets you add a static IP address to the cryptographic identifier for each node, so you can use IP-based apps over the Reticulum network without having to reverse engineer anything. That's pretty smart, reducing the barrier to entry for this potentially life-saving networking stack that's perfect for disaster rescue and recovery missions and more.

ZeroTier
See at Official Site

Make your own mesh network with encryption and resilient networking

Reticulum isn't the only alternative network stack out there, but it has some real promise in the sheer number of devices that can run it. Think mesh networks for remote villages or those underserved communities where robust internet infrastructure has yet to arrive. It enables free, encrypted messaging over radio communications, or almost anything else that can carry a signal, and connects each device into a unified mesh network for the community.

item.title: Two of Sony's greatest exclusives finally broke free of the PS4, so I remastered them with DLSS 5
item.itunes:title: Two of Sony's greatest exclusives finally broke free of the PS4, so I remastered them with DLSS 5
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's funny how two of PlayStation's greatest experiences ever have also been its most poorly served. FromSoftware's Bloodborne came to the PS5, but it never got a remaster, remake, or even a 60FPS patch. Meanwhile, P.T., Hideo Kojima's legendary playable teaser for the canceled Silent Hills, was de-listed forever from the PlayStation Store in 2015, just eight months after release.

Both of these games deserve better than being shackled to the hardware they debuted on. Now, however, vibe-coding is helping hundreds of players create native PC projects through decompilation and recompilation, and they're taking console relics and throwing modern rendering technology at them.

Getting both of these games to run on my PC through my own files was a feat in and of itself, but I was far more interested in the new "magical" kid on the block — DLSS 5.

I ran DLSS 5 on my PS2 games, and they finally looked like I remembered them

Nostalgia, meet neural rendering

11
By  Samarveer Singh

2014 console exclusives and DLSS 5 work like a charm, apparently

The secret sauce is OptiScaler, of course

Getting P.T. running natively on my PC was one thing, but injecting DLSS 5 neural rendering into a game that predates the technology by twelve years was an entirely different challenge. For P.T., I was fairly interested in seeing what happens when I introduced DLSS 5 to a game that never anticipated anything like it. For Bloodborne, I could have done this using the ShadPS4 emulator at any time during the last month, much like I did with my other PlayStation 3 games.

Bloodborne on PC uses a dedicated translation layer that lets its original PS4 executable run on a Windows or Linux PC's x86-64 processor. So, it's not completely a native project, but it's faster, smoother, and much more direct than traditional PS4 emulation software, all without being a complete source-level port. This "native" port for the game has support for DLSS with uncapped framerates, which gave me a lot more performance to work with before paying the usual neural rendering tax, which more than halves the performance of a game with each neural rendering layer you throw at it.

Thankfully, OptiScaler has evolved into a rather ingenious workaround — it let me inject Nvidia's neural rendering capabilities into games that were never designed to support them. Problem is, DLSS 5 just isn't conventional upscaling. The neural rendering model uses scene information to transform a game's appearance, and alters how details, materials, and lighting are perceived. Outside of official supported titles, using DLSS 5 requires plenty of additional plumbing and elbow grease, and that's where community-built OptiScaler with neural rendering support comes in.

I unlocked RTX 50-series features on my RTX 4070 Ti, and Nvidia's GPU generations don't make sense anymore

My old card is gaining new features it isn't supposed to have

By  Samarveer Singh

P.T. looked great with DLSS 5, but I couldn't quite see the point

The FOX Engine game remains magical over a decade later

P.T. on PC is a full native PC port, with its game logic rebuilt entirely in C++ and a Vulkan renderer loading the original assets from your own PS4 files. This does, however, require that you somehow own a PlayStation 4 device with the game files installed for P.T., which, luckily, I had from all the way back in 2014.

The PC port, with its ray traced lighting and shadows, already looked miles better than the original game on my PlayStation 4, but with two neural rendering passes added to the frame, P.T. looked better than ever before. Since this native PC port of P.T. supports DLSS Super Resolution as well as DLSS Frame Generation, running OptiScaler along with Neural Rendering DLL files was a piece of cake.

The textures looked like they could've been made yesterday, but truth be told, the FOX Engine was doing so much of the work here that even the original PS4's graphical settings looked fantastic at 1440p with DLSS Quality.

Regardless, the game definitely got a new coat of paint, and dare I say, it became scarier. With more realistic floors, walls, and objects than ever before, it got all the more terrifying when these same assets became hostile towards me the more I explored the same two corridors of the Playable Teaser. Yet for all the visual polish DLSS 5 added, I couldn't quite shake the feeling that P.T. was already doing most things right.

Reading DLSS 5's source code finally made sense of the neural rendering complaints

DLSS 5 really does work like an AI filter, and the source code proves it

4
By  Samarveer Singh

DLSS 5 was a resounding triumph for Bloodborne

Yharnam has never looked this good

DLSS 5 was definitely a success with P.T., but it was with Bloodborne that it truly shined. Yharnam was completely revamped, with every single building in the Gothic-Victorian city looking drop-dead gorgeous. DLSS 5's neural rendering completely refreshed the graphics while keeping the visuals as close to the original aesthetic as possible. This was perhaps the clearest example of preserving the original artistic vision while still truly blowing you away with the neural rendering's take on the cobbled streets, enemy characters, player outfits, and the entire surrounding environment.

The difference was magnificent, and clearly, DLSS 5 had plenty of visual information to work with. The city retained its grimy, decaying aesthetic, which, for over a decade, has defined its identity. However, its materials and finer details took on a whole new character under neural rendering. Bloodborne felt like a much more compelling demonstration of what Nvidia's neural rendering could bring to an older game.

Bloodborne gave me plenty of trouble, though. The native PC launcher seemed a little too adamant to not let me run OptiScaler. Thankfully, ReShade, along with one of its most popular community add-ons, Deep Fried Chicken, helped me run neural processing passes on BloodBorne. There were certainly some hoops to jump through, but boy was it worth the reward when I finally managed to get things running.

I put DLSS 5 on my entire desktop, and it showed me neural rendering's real limits

DLSS 5 Live Flow promised to transform my desktop — here's what actually happened

3
By  Samarveer Singh

The best days of game preservation may still lie ahead

Decompilation and recompilation are becoming two of gaming's most exciting preservation tools, letting enthusiasts bring beloved console games to PC without waiting for Sony to remember its exclusives exist. Vibe-coding with tools like Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex is accelerating development at what seems like light speed, which is why we're seeing increasingly ambitious projects emerge.

Preserving a game used to mean keeping an old console running, or hoping that its digital storefront stayed online. Now, that's changing faster than ever. The decompilation and recompilation community is getting stronger by the day, with increasingly ambitious projects that we once thought were inseparable from their original hardware.

That's what excites me the most about this whole movement. Every successful project makes the next seemingly impossible undertaking a little less daunting, opening doors for games that might otherwise disappear into obscurity. If this is where we're at today, I can't wait to see what's next.

item.title: I fixed my smart TV’s slow video streaming without upgrading my internet
item.itunes:title: I fixed my smart TV’s slow video streaming without upgrading my internet
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Nothing ruins a movie night faster than endless buffering, blurry visuals, and streaming apps that take forever to load. That’s exactly what I was dealing with on my TCL Google TV. At first, I blamed my internet connection and even considered upgrading to a faster plan.

However, everything worked perfectly fine on my phone, MacBook, and Windows desktop. That’s when I realized my internet speed wasn’t a problem. I dug into my TV’s settings and network setup, and a few simple changes made a noticeable difference.

I checked my TV’s actual internet speed

Switching Wi-Fi bands made a difference

Before upgrading my internet plan, I ran a network test on my Android TV. My phone and laptop were getting excellent download speeds, but I wanted to know how much bandwidth my Smart TV was actually receiving. Here, I used a third-party app called Analiti to do the job.

If you don’t want to deal with a third-party app, head to Netflix > Get Help > Check your network menu and glance over the network speeds. To my surprise, the TV was getting slower speeds even though it was connected to the same network. That’s when I headed to the Wi-Fi menu on my TV and found that it was connected to my home Wi-Fi’s 2.4GHz frequency.

While it offers better range, it can become crowded with other devices, including home gadgets and neighboring Wi-Fi networks. The 5GHz band generally offers faster speeds and less interference. I switched to 5GHz, and the difference was noticeable. Videos started loading more consistently, and I experienced fewer hiccups during streaming sessions.

I stopped ignoring these underrated smart TV features, and you should too

These features aren't always enabled or widely known — it's time to change that

2
By  Tanveer Singh

I optimized my router’s placement

It also plays a major role in deciding internet speeds

I had always assumed that as long as my smart TV showed a strong Wi-Fi signal, that router’s placement didn’t matter much. However, I realized that signal strength alone doesn’t tell the whole story. Walls, furniture, electronic devices, and even the router’s position can affect connection quality and streaming performance.

My router was tucked away in a corner, surrounded by furniture. It wasn’t an ideal location, especially when I needed a stable 5GHz connection. item.title: The 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 is the only SBC I'd tell a beginner to buy right now
item.itunes:title: The 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 is the only SBC I'd tell a beginner to buy right now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
SBC prices aren’t what they used to be, and that makes your purchase decision tougher than before. It wasn’t too long ago that you could snag the cheapest usable Raspberry Pi (Zero 2 W) for $15. The latest iteration, Raspberry Pi 5 4GB, retailed for $60, while the 8GB memory variant launched for $80. A 2GB memory edition of the board was revealed soon after for $50. The 8GB memory variant looked like a sweet deal until AI advancements ruined it. Memory prices have increased, making the boards way more expensive than before.

The makers recently launched a 1GB edition of the Raspberry Pi 5 for $45. It has double the amount of memory you get with a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. There’s also a 1GB edition of the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, but I cannot recommend it. Here’s why the 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 makes sense for a beginner in these testing times.

Don't fall for an older board

Sheer waste of money

The biggest 1GB memory rival in the lineup is the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B. It launched in 2019 and at that time $35 felt like a lot. It's great that the makers haven't increased its price. When the 2GB Raspberry Pi 5 was available for $50, nobody paid attention to it. The 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 is $10 more expensive than the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, while the 2GB variant is almost $80 now. So, the decision boils down to the 1GB edition of both boards.

I wouldn't suggest going with the old Raspberry Pi 4 Model B because its hardware holds it back. To save $10, you're sacrificing a lot of things that are necessary for modern-day computing projects. The biggest motivation to buy a Raspberry Pi 5 is obviously the improved processor. It can prove useful for demanding self-hosted tools and modern workflows. The port configuration remains the same, but you get the option to add an NVMe SSD to the Raspberry Pi 5.

A 29MB AI model is the most useful thing I've run on my Raspberry Pi 5, and it doesn't need an AI HAT

The tiniest AI model I've tried on a Raspberry Pi 5 is only 29MB, and it's surprisingly handy

By  Ayush Pande

It requires a specific variant but it's miles better than relying on an SD card for your OS and tools. I've had SD cards fail multiple times, and if I were to buy a new board, the one with maximum storage options would be a priority. You can boot the OS from an external USB on both the boards, but it makes the setup cluttered.

The Raspberry Pi 5 needs a HAT module to connect an SSD, but you don't need to buy one instantly. You can try other storage options and understand their constraints before upgrading to it. If you pick a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, you cannot upgrade to an NVMe SSD in the future.

1GB memory capacity feels insufficient

But you can learn a lot from it

In an era where your smartphone has 8–12 GB of memory, laptops come with a similar capacity; the 1GB memory model might feel insufficient. For an experienced user, the memory capacity should be a little higher than the overall requirement. If the prices drop to the original levels, I would suggest going for a 4GB or 8GB Raspberry Pi 5. But that's a future-proofing approach, and it isn't feasible for a beginner.

There are multiple things that you can accomplish with just 1GB of memory. I have built several projects using a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, which has only 512MB memory. Compared to that, the Raspberry Pi 5 has double the capacity, which means tools like Nextcloud, Home Assistant, and Jellyfin can work. The board might not be capable of hardcore transcoding or other machine learning tasks due to limited memory. Yet, most of the self-hosted tools that draw a beginner to the SBC realm will run smoothly on the 1GB variant.

My Raspberry Pi 5 paid for itself in less than a year thanks to Docker containers, but that's almost impossible now

It's just too expensive these days

2
By  Ayush Pande

It’s one of the key learnings when using an SBC because you have to focus on minimizing the overall resource consumption. Rather than installing a full-scale GUI desktop, you can go with a lightweight option like DietPi for memory management. It needs less memory, leaving plenty for Docker and the tools you want to use. You can try multiple software alternatives, check which ones work without hiccups, and build a truly useful server with it.

Another overlooked aspect is memory generation. The Raspberry Pi Zero 2W uses LPDDR2 and the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B uses LPDDR4 memory. Both are older-generation memory with slower bandwidth and lag behind the LPDDR4X of the Raspberry Pi 5. It’s more of a performance improvement that some apps might benefit from while using less power.

Start small and scale up

It’s still a capable SBC

The 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 is not a weak SBC. It shares the same hardware as other models in the series with a lower memory capacity. You cannot use it as a regular PC and install a GUI OS on it. But you can run most of the self-hosted tools on it without any problems. Think of it as a challenge to build and maintain a small-scale server with limited memory. No other SBC in the Raspberry Pi family supports NVMe drives, which is an additional perk of the SBC.

Once you hit a wall with the memory capacity, you can repurpose the SBC for a single use case, like a Nextcloud server. It's even possible to pool it in a cluster along with other powerful SBCs using Docker Swarm or other orchestration tools. The board also supports AI HATs, which means even if you have less onboard memory, you can work on AI projects. The AI HATs with their own memory would be apt for your 1GB Raspberry Pi 5.

The most obvious pick

None of us can control the SBC or component prices. If you really want to learn embedded computing or build servers out of small computers, there’s no better, budget-friendly option than the 1GB Raspberry Pi 5. It won’t become your primary server, which is something every beginner hopes for with their first SBC purchase. Use it as a stepping stone to get into the world of small computing devices, and build projects that serve a role in your home.

Raspberry Pi 5
CPU
Arm Cortex-A76 (quad-core, 2.4GHz)
Memory
Up to 8GB LPDDR4X SDRAM

item.title: LibreOffice opens files from the '90s that Microsoft Office now refuses to touch
item.itunes:title: LibreOffice opens files from the '90s that Microsoft Office now refuses to touch
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Microsoft Office has been a mainstay since it launched, and since that time, its file structure has changed. That's expected, but it has changed to the point where newer versions of the software cannot open files created by older versions. For example, Microsoft’s support documentation says PowerPoint 2007 and every version since are unable to open a file saved in the PowerPoint 95 format. LibreOffice, the default Office alternative on Linux, opens it on the first try with no configuration necessary. Across Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, Microsoft has spent nearly two decades walling off the early versions of its own formats, and a free, open-source suite has quietly become the more dependable way to read them.

LibreOffice once again slams Microsoft for using "lock-in" with Office files

item.title: Buying all your NAS drives in one batch is a mistake, and I mix brands and dates on purpose
item.itunes:title: Buying all your NAS drives in one batch is a mistake, and I mix brands and dates on purpose
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I buy a new NAS, I’ve got an entire checklist of things I go through before making the deal. The RAM, for instance, is something I pay a lot of attention to when I plan to arm it with a ZFS-laden distribution. Likewise, unless I’m planning to put together a simple OpenMediaVault server, I ensure that the CPU powering my storage hub has the x86 (or x86-64, for pedantic folks) architecture.

On the drive front, I always aim for units with at least four HDD bays, and if it’s within the budget, a handful of M.2 slots for the boot OS. Since we’re on this subject, I’m also quite staunch about checking the S.M.A.R.T. metrics and running stress tests on brand-new drives before I shove them into my NAS. But above all else, I always ensure that I mix and match HDDs from different manufacturers when I order new ones for my NAS units.

Correlated batch failure is a real problem for bulk HDD purchases

Unfortunately, my NAS setup isn’t robust enough to survive multiple drive failures

Unlike PSUs, storage drives are often among the first NAS components that bite the dust. Hard drives, in particular, are prone to mechanical failure, as they rely on physical components like platters, motors, and arms that are prone to degradation after years of use. Certain S.M.A.R.T. metrics can be telltale signs of a failing HDD, but you could just as easily have a drive function well for years, only for it to ascend to tech heaven the next day due to some random manufacturing defect.

Now, let’s say you bought a couple of HDDs belonging to the same batch in bulk. This means that all the drives in your pool will age together, and essentially get exposed to the same amount of stress. This increases the chances of your drives failing at the same time, which can be a death sentence for many home labbers (including yours truly). Not to mention, hard drives manufactured in a batch tend to share physical and firmware issues, which can cause the same defect to hit multiple HDDs simultaneously.

Unfortunately, typical consumer NAS units aren’t equipped to handle simultaneous drive failures. I’ve got a RAID 10 storage pool, which can only tolerate up to two dead HDDs, and that too if they belong to different mirrored sets. In the more conventional RAID solutions that can only tolerate a maximum of one failed drive, correlated batch failure becomes a real threat to your storage pool.

I even pick drives from different batches for my Proxmox clusters

Since I’d rather avoid dealing with simultaneous drive failures, I follow the iron code of grabbing drives from different manufacturers altogether. If I stuck to a single manufacturer and switched vendors, there’s still a slim possibility that my new storage companions might belong to the same batch.

I’ve got a handful of server nodes as well, and although all the data from these workstations gets backed up to my local (and remote) NAS units, I still follow the same principle of picking HDDs from different manufacturers when I want to create some storage pools for my cluster experiments. After all, my high-availability Proxmox cluster would be rendered useless if the ZFS pools on two nodes go down at the same time.

That said, I’d never mix drives with different specs

I don’t want to deal with the annoying issues of a hybrid pool

Before you call me out for choosing different hard drives for my storage and virtualization servers, let me confirm that the differences only extend to the manufacturing date and the company making the HDD. For the rest of the specifications, including the RPM, cache size, and (most importantly) capacity, I take great care to ensure that all HDDs remain identical.

Yes, I’m aware that Unraid and a couple of other distributions already support storage pools built with completely different HDDs, but I’m a TrueNAS user first and foremost. Although the latter has added provisions to combine different capacity drives in recent updates, I’d have to contend with ZFS limiting the usable storage of the vdev to the size of the smallest drive.

Adding more redundancy provides an extra layer of safety for my precious files

Since I’d like to reduce the chances of my precious storage pools getting rendered unusable, I rely on snapshot replication alongside my HDD-specific iron code. To be more precise, I’ve got a spare NAS receiving snapshots from my local storage server every once in a while. That way, even if I somehow end up with more than one failed drive on my local workstation, I’d be able to recover all the data from my remote server. And if this situation gets flipped around and my offsite NAS gets afflicted with dead drives, I can remotely activate the hot spares and initiate the recovery tasks from my local PC.

item.title: This one Windows 11 update made my PC faster and consume less RAM, and I didn't change a single setting
item.itunes:title: This one Windows 11 update made my PC faster and consume less RAM, and I didn't change a single setting
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Microsoft has caused enough anxiety with every Patch Tuesday and routine updates that have borked one aspect or another of Windows 11 for users this year, and as such, the latest 26H2 update feels like a breath of fresh air. Perhaps for the first time in ages, I installed a Windows update and watched things get considerably better instead of breaking something.

If you're on Windows 11, you'll notice little things that matter after this update. The Start menu will snap open faster, Search will be more responsive, and apps will launch without a half-second stall that you've likely grown accustomed to. Perhaps the very best part of it all is that this time, there are no tweaks, no secret tricks, no changing power plans, and certainly no tinkering with the registry editor to feel the change. 26H2 is an update that's done right, and if you haven't updated yet, here's why you should.

The Low Latency Profile made my PC snappier than it has ever been

Windows 11 now has a faster way to wake up the CPU

When we think of productivity, our minds often go to the tools we use, how effectively they can help us manage our time, and the workflows that we spend time perfecting and building around them. The feel of the operating system rarely warrants a thought here, but it's one aspect that determines how productive we can be with our tools.

What most users don't realize is that the responsiveness of an OS directly influences engagement and productivity. In 1982, IBM found that system response times under 400 milliseconds were key to keeping users engaged, and this is known as the Doherty Threshold. Crossing that line means that a user's attention could start to drift, and Windows 11 has famously spent most of its life on the wrong side of it. If you go through older user forums, you can find complaints about the Start menu feeling sluggish, slow Search results, and app launches that seem to take forever.

Microsoft's way to remedy this is the Low Latency Profile. On 26H2, when Windows detects a latency-sensitive action like opening the Start menu or launching an app, it briefly pushes the CPU close to its maximum clock for one to three seconds, which is enough to get the shell element or application window on screen. The feature first shipped in the June 2026 security update (KB5094126), with the August update extending it to app launches. The 26H2 update flips the switch, enabling the feature for all supported systems.

Early data from reviewers looks promising. In a test, Windows Latest reported that native apps like Edge and Outlook launched about 40% faster, with the Start menu and other UI elements responding up to 70% quicker. item.itunes:summary:
Windows 11 may have done a lot of great things, but many others are fairly contentious, and it's easy to miss how things used to work. Thankfully, there are a few tools out there that can restore the classic behaviors of Windows 11, and one of the best is ExplorerPatcher.

There are other great customization tools out there, such as Start11 and StartAllBack, and while they're great, they also cost money. ExplorerPatcher is a free alternative, and it's a great one at that. It can restore things like the Start menu, taskbar, and more, and after setting it up, I have to wonder why I didn't install it sooner.

The Windows 10 Start menu is still better

Straight to what you need

Right off the bat, being able to restore the Windows 10 Start menu with ExplorerPatcher is an extremely welcome change, and the biggest reason to use this app, in my opinion. Many celebrated the death of live tiles with Windows 11, but I could never get behind that because you had so much more freedom, space, and control.

For starters, the menu is almost completely resizable, so you can adjust the height and width to your heart's content. And sure, using large tiles in the pinned area wasted some space, but you could easily resize tiles and fit dozens of apps on a single screen. On top of that, the All apps list was always visible and ready to be scrolled without affecting the pinned area. You can get to less frequently used apps much more quickly.

Ranking all the Windows Start menus, from worst to best

The Start menu has evolved (and devolved) quite a number of times since its debut on Windows 95

1
By  Ayush Pande

In recent months, Microsoft has tried to address some of this feedback, and the all apps list is now directly in the main view, just below the pinned area. It's a welcome improvement, but it doesn't address all the other advantages of the Windows 10 Start menu, so I still highly recommend ExplorerPatcher for this change alone.

The taskbar gets some upgrades, too

You can still get the weather (sometimes)

ExplorerPatcher also lets you restore the taskbar to the Windows 10 style, meaning you get individual, clickable icons for things like Wi-Fi and battery. I'm not heavily invested in these smaller changes, but what I really like is the weather widget you get with ExplorerPatcher.

This replaces the official widgets implementation in Windows 11, which is heavily based on web technologies and can feel both slow and like a resource hog, while also bombarding you with information you don't care about. Here, you get a sleek, beautiful weather widget, and that's it. Sometimes, less is more, and this looks great.

Well, when it works, that is. I've periodically had issues with this widget, and at writing time, it doesn't seem to be able to properly display data. It's possible that an update will restore the functionality, but it's hard to say when or if that will happen. The app was last updated in July of this year, so hopefully a new version is coming soon to address this issue.

3 ways you can take your Windows 11 Taskbar back in time with this fantastic retro app

Retrobar is a powerful app that transforms your Taskbar into one from an earlier version of Windows

By  Daryl Baxter

Otherwise, many of the Windows 11 flyouts are also replaced with Windows 10 equivalents, which match the respective system tray icons, but in some cases, you can even use the Windows 7 version of those flyouts. And in most cases, you can also make it so that clicking one of these icons takes you directly to the respective page in Control Panel or the Settings app, so you get a little more control over the experience.

The Ribbon is back

File Explorer gets better too

The last major thing I love about ExplorerPatcher is that it can also restore the File Explorer UI to how it was in Windows 10 (and 8) with the Ribbon UI. The Ribbon puts all the options you could possibly want right in front of you, so everything from copying and deleting files, renaming them, or just selecting them is more immediately accessible at a glance.

Plus, with the different tabs in the Ribbon, you can easily do things like view hidden items, show file extensions, and more, all at a quick glance with an easy-to-navigate UI. All of these features are still in Windows 11, but the more simplified format of the new File Explorer feels less intuitive at times, and I much prefer the Ribbon.

The big downside here is that by restoring the Windows 10-style UI, you also remove Windows 11 features; most notably, tab support. It's not a small sacrifice, but it's one I'm still willing to make.

5 great features Windows 8 introduced that it doesn't get enough credit for

We hated it, but there's a lot worth loving

1
By  João Carrasqueira

Then there are smaller things

Though some are hit or miss

In addition to these big features that make ExplorerPatcher worth it to me, there are a lot of extra tweaking options you might appreciate, too. For example, you can change the style of the window switcher that appears when pressing Alt+Tab, making it more like Windows 10 or going even simpler and removing visual indicators altogether.

There are a couple of smaller things like disabling certain keyboard shortcuts, such as Windows + F for the Feedback Hub, or preventing certain system links from being redirected from the Control Panel to the new Settings app. It's nice to get these little bonus features, even if I don't think they're a huge reason to use the app.

4 reasons to customize Windows 11 with StartAllBack

StartAllBack is a super useful customization app for Windows 11. If you're not using it yet, here's why you should be.

By  João Carrasqueira

Some features seem to have either been broken or fixed in Windows itself in the latest releases. For example, there's still an option here for overriding the Windows + C shortcut that was used for Teams in the original Windows 11 release, but that shortcut has since been replaced, and pressing it now equates to the Copilot button, which you can remap in the Settings app. There are also features related to Windows Spotlight that don't seem to work on the latest releases, either.

You should check out ExplorerPatcher

Even with the downsides, ExplorerPatcher is an amazing app if you're a Windows 11 user. Some of the Windows 10 elements that can be restored with this tool are much better for me than what Windows 11 offers out of the box. Plus, original additions like the weather widget are also a significant improvement over Microsoft's own, at least when they work.

While updates tend to be slow, the app seems to be actively supported, so any issues should be ironed out in future updates, and it's always worth checking out what it can do for you.

All of these features are still in Windows 11, but the more simplified format of the new File Explorer feels less intuitive at times, and I much prefer the Ribbon.

The big downside here is that by restoring the Windows 10-style UI, you also remove Windows 11 features; most notably, tab support. It's not a small sacrifice, but it's one I'm still willing to make.

In addition to these big features that make ExplorerPatcher worth it to me, there are a lot of extra tweaking options you might appreciate, too. For example, you can change the style of the window switcher that appears when pressing Alt+Tab, making it more like Windows 10 or going even simpler and removing visual indicators altogether.

There are a couple of smaller things like disabling certain keyboard shortcuts, such as Windows + F for the Feedback Hub, or preventing certain system links from being redirected from the Control Panel to the new Settings app. It's nice to get these little bonus features, even if I don't think they're a huge reason to use the app.

Some features seem to have either been broken or fixed in Windows itself in the latest releases. Even with the downsides, ExplorerPatcher is an amazing app if you're a Windows 11 user. item.itunes:title: I ignored these useful Plex features for years, and now I can’t live without them
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've used Plex since the 2010s, and over the years, the platform has added several new features. I noticed some and was excited to start using them right away. However, some cool features slipped under the radar. Once I started digging into lesser-known Plex features, I discovered several I'd ignored for a long time.

These abilities didn't get much fanfare, or I missed them. Now that I'm acclimated to these features, I plan to use them to improve my self-hosted (and free streaming TV) media experience.

Live TV

Connecting an HD Antenna via a tuner

This isn't a hidden feature; it is clearly labeled in the UI, but I didn't know how well it worked until I tried it. When I think of self-hosted media platforms, I think of ripping my Blu-ray discs and serving my movies and shows throughout the house. I don't think much about live TV and overlooked the feature for years.

It's mainly because of my location and the poor OTA reception I get. But once I decided that paying $90/month for livestreaming TV was too much for one NFL game a week, I looked into a cheap tuner and a digital antenna. I at least wanted local channels that carry my local team's games on screens throughout my house.

Connecting the tuner to my router and letting Plex discover it was a cinch. Plus, Plex Pass (which I complain about a lot) provides a built-in program guide that populates automatically. It's easier than Jellyfin, which requires a separate XMLTV guide source and additional configuration. I can also use the section to create my own self-hosted media channels for a TV-like streaming experience. Combining Tunarr or ErsatzTV channels with free over-the-air stations in the guide is a fun, unique way to watch television on Plex.

I've stopped recommending Plex to newcomers, because Jellyfin is ready for families now

The gap between the Plex and Jellyfin's polish is no longer a chasm

36
By  Samarveer Singh

Universal search

Discover content from a single UI the easy way

When I stream my own media on Plex via my Nvidia Shield Pro, or stream other content, I often want to find something related. I use the Apple TV a lot too, and have a bad habit of using its own stand-alone search function. On the Shield TV Pro or another device, I use its search feature to look for shows. However, I don't have to leave Plex to find content because it includes universal search.

Streaming content has become so fragmented that it's hard to know where everything lives. Universal search lets me discover the shows I want to watch and tells me which service has them. After a query, it also displays where I can purchase a digital version of a movie or show I want to watch. It won't make headlines, and most Plex users already know about it. However, it helps me break the bad content-search habits I learned from years of using Apple TV, and it lets me spend more time in Plex and less elsewhere.

Building collections

A better way to organize my growing media library

Like most self-hosters, my media library keeps growing weekly. So much so that I ran out of storage and resurrected an old server to add more space. An overlooked feature that lets me better organize my movies and shows is adding existing content to collections. It groups my titles without moving the files into separate libraries for each category or franchise.

For instance, I have all the John Wick films on my Plex server. I can easily add them all to a collection for easier access. I open my media library and select the movie posters. Then I select Add to > Add to Collection, and name it. I can also add other content to the collection later. I can do this with more than movies; I use collections to manually curate collections of TV shows, music videos, and more. I can organize content into categories like Westerns, Dramas, Fantasy, and others.

Once I curate collections, I can search them, which makes finding my large collection of shows much simpler. I can use the feature to organize any content I self-host on my Plex server better. The controls let me reduce clutter by hiding content and using the smart collections feature to organize it automatically. For large libraries, this is a helpful, underused Plex resource.

I stopped scrolling through my Plex library for hours after finding this open-source recommendation app

Shortlist does what Plex refuses to: turn my massive library into something I actually want to watch.

Still, you may have missed other features, like collections or the benefits of live TV with an HD antenna and a cheap tuner. Free Plex companion apps can also improve the server experience. What are some of your favorites?
